entries.title: Predictable AI spend in BigQuery: Introducing cost management for generative AI functions
entries.summary: The generative AI functions in BigQuery (AI.GENERATE, AI.IF, AI.CLASSIFY, AI.SCORE, and more) bring large language models (LLMs) directly into your SQL, so a single query can classify millions of support tickets or score each product review for sentiment. However, because these functions are billed by the token, scaling them across massive datasets highlights the importance of managing your budget
entries.content:
Tushar Jaiswal

Software Engineer

Alicia Williams

Developer Advocate

The generative AI functions in BigQuery (

AI.GENERATE
, 
AI.IF
, 
AI.CLASSIFY
, 
AI.SCORE
, and more) bring large language models (LLMs) directly into your SQL, so a single query can classify millions of support tickets or score each product review for sentiment. However, because these functions are billed by the token, scaling them across massive datasets highlights the importance of managing your budget proactively. 

We recently announced the general availability (GA) of token-based cost management for BigQuery generative AI functions: daily quotas that let administrators set self-serve guardrails on AI token consumption, so teams can innovate while staying within your budget. In this blog, we provide an overview of cost management for BigQuery generative AI functions, walk through a few practical examples, and share resources to help you get started. Let’s jump in.  

Quotas for managing costs

Four daily quotas, managed through the Google Cloud Identity and Access Management (IAM) quota system, provide controls at the project level and the per-user level. Per-user limits apply to each user within a project, not across your organization.

Key details:

  • The quotas are global. Usage is summed across all regions, so costs can't pile up unnoticed in a region you weren't watching.

  • Output quotas include "thinking" tokens. Reasoning tokens count toward your output quota, just as they count toward your Gemini platform bill.

Which functions are covered?

The quotas apply to these BigQuery functions that perform LLM-backed generation:

  • AI.GENERATE

  • AI.GENERATE_TABLE

  • AI.GENERATE_TEXT
    (and its alias 
    ML.GENERATE_TEXT
    )

  • AI.CLASSIFY

  • AI.IF

  • AI.SCORE

  • AI.AGG

What's not covered: Embedding functions such as 

AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING
(also available as 
ML.GENERATE_EMBEDDING
) and 
AI.EMBED
 are not subject to these quotas, because they run on different, substantially cheaper models.

Managing your quotas

Administrators can view and adjust the quotas directly in the Google Cloud console as workloads change, with no support case required.

  • Navigate to IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

  • Filter by service and select BigQuery API.

  • Sort by the Name column to bring the four AI quotas to the top.

Locating the gen AI token quotas in IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

4. Find the quota, for example AI input tokens per day.

5. Open the three-dot menu and choose Edit quota.

From there:

  • To tighten cost control, lower a quota. This takes effect immediately with no approval needed.

  • To support higher usage, request an increase from the same page. Many requests are auto-approved; larger increases may go through a quick review.

Editing a gen AI token quota in IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

You'll need the right permissions. You need one of: Owner, Editor, Quota Administrator (

roles/servicemanagement.quotaAdmin
), or Service Usage Admin (
roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin
).

Prefer automation? You can also manage these quotas programmatically through the Cloud Quotas API, the 

gcloud
CLI, and Terraform to apply consistent guardrails across projects.

Monitoring usage

Beyond setting limits, the Quotas & System Limits page displays your historical token consumption so you can quickly detect spikes and right-size your budgets. Use these trends to see how new generative AI workloads and data pipelines affect your overall token usage.

Daily project-level token usage for a gen AI token quota in IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

Longer-term usage graph with selectable 7-day, 14-day, 30-day, and custom ranges.

For a step-by-step walkthrough, see the BigQuery documentation on controlling costs with token quotas.

Token quotas vs. billing spend caps

Token quotas aren't the only cost guardrail in Google Cloud.

  • Token quotas (this feature) are preventive and AI-specific. BigQuery tracks token usage during query execution and stops work close to the limit, with separate limits per project and per user.

  • Cloud Billing spend caps operate on dollars at the project and service level and can automatically block usage when a threshold is reached. They're a broad, financial backstop rather than a precise usage control, and because enforcement is not instant, some overages are incurred.

Use token quotas as your first line of defense for AI spend, and a spend cap as a project-wide safety net.

How enforcement works

Quotas are enforced by stopping work rather than letting a query run past your limit. A query is rejected up front with a 

QuotaExceeded
error only if a quota it needs is already exhausted. Otherwise, it starts, and if a quota runs out mid-query, BigQuery stops sending new LLM calls:

  • Functions that support 

    max_error_ratio
    (such as 
    AI.IF
    ) return partial results if unprocessed rows stay within the ratio, and otherwise fail.

  • General-purpose functions (such as 

    AI.GENERATE
    ) still succeed. Skipped rows have no generated value, and their 
    status
    field contains the quota-exceeded error.

For details, see quota enforcement behavior in the documentation.

Sizing your input data: 
AI.COUNT_TOKENS

To choose quota values, it helps to know how much text your workloads send to a model. The 

AI.COUNT_TOKENS
function helps with this.

AI.COUNT_TOKENS
returns the number of tokens a model's tokenizer produces for a text string, without making a billable generation call. Run it over a column to measure your input data:

The count is a lower bound on input tokens. It doesn't include output or thinking tokens, the instructions each AI function adds around your input, or non-text inputs such as images. Use it to:

  • Gauge the input side of a workload before you launch it.

  • Right-size your quotas together with a small sample run that measures actual input and output usage.

  • Translate tokens into dollars using the published Gemini platform pricing for your model.

From tokens to budget: a worked example

Suppose you want to keep a project's daily AI spend around $100 with the Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite model. As of today's published pricing (BigQuery processes in batch which provides a 50% discount):

  • Input tokens: $0.125 per 1 million tokens

  • Output tokens (response + reasoning): $0.75 per 1 million tokens

If a small sample run shows an average 100:1 input-to-output token ratio, you can solve for a daily budget:

Solving gives about 754 million input tokens and 7.54 million output tokens per day. Set AI input tokens per day and AI output tokens per day to these values to hold the project near $100/day. If a project uses models with different prices, budget per model or blend the rates.

Best practices for managing AI cost

  • Start with per-user quotas. They stop one user or runaway experiment from draining the project's budget.

  • Measure before you scale. Use 

    AI.COUNT_TOKENS
    to size your input, then check a small sample run in the usage chart before setting limits.

  • Mind the output side. Output tokens cost more. Where a function accepts 

    max_output_tokens
    , set it to bound generation length.

  • Monitor and iterate. Adjust limits as real usage and budgets change.

Get started

Token-based cost management is available now. To begin:

  • Open IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits in the Google Cloud Console and filter by BigQuery API.

  • Review the four AI-related token quotas and set limits that match your budget.

  • Use 

    AI.COUNT_TOKENS
    to size your input data.

For the full details, see the documentation on controlling generative AI costs.

With token-based guardrails in place, your teams can use generative AI in BigQuery with the cost predictability your organization needs.

Welcome to the first Cloud CISO Perspectives for October 2026. Today, Stephanie Kiel explains the latest on our approach to post-quantum cryptography, and shares a new tool to help CISOs and executives prepare their organizations for PQC.

As with all Cloud CISO Perspectives, the contents of this newsletter are posted to the Google Cloud blog. If you’re reading this on the website and you’d like to receive the email version, you can subscribe here.

New Gemini Notebook can help CISOs and policymakers prepare for PQC

By Stephanie Kiel, Head of Cloud Security Policy, Government Affairs and Public Policy, Google Cloud

Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is one of the most urgent security shifts of the decade — and one of the easiest to tune out. For security leaders and policymakers, the research is dense, scattered across papers and engineering blogs, and can be challenging to turn into action.

To help, we're launching Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography, a public Gemini Notebook that brings Google's PQC research, engineering blogs, and migration guidance together in one place. Ask it questions, listen to an audio overview, or test yourself with flashcards, and quickly get up to speed on the quantum threat.

Why PQC matters now

Quantum computing is rapidly moving from theory to reality. Our Willow chip and Quantum Echoes algorithm mark substantial progress, and Google research estimates that breaking ECDLP-256 and RSA-2048 encryption — the public-key cryptography schemes protecting much of our online data — would require around 500,000 and 1 million imperfect quantum computer components (noisy qubits), respectively.

To help, we're launching Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography, a public Gemini Notebook that brings Google's PQC research, engineering blogs, and migration guidance together in one place.

This research has consequences now. It indicates that today’s online security is more vulnerable to future quantum computers than previously thought.

In Store Now, Decrypt Later attacks, adversaries may steal encrypted data now and wait to decrypt it once a sufficiently powerful quantum computer exists. Data that we’ve long considered sensitive — health records, financial data, intellectual property, and government secrets — is already at risk. 

With continued advances in architecture, quantum algorithms, and quantum error correction shrinking future quantum hardware requirements, waiting to upgrade our digital locks is not a viable option. To help organizations stay ahead of the curve, Google has published a migration timeline noting our plans to transition to PQC by 2029, and we urge others to consider the same.

As the technology advances, policymakers should consider urging critical infrastructure owners and operators to recognize condensed timelines, and build PQC readiness into existing risk mitigation plans. We also recommend governments engage with global counterparts to promote a harmonized approach to standards development, and include technical and security experts in the building of policy and regulatory requirements focused on quantum safety.

Google's PQC expertise, in one notebook

The Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography notebook turns years of Google expertise into an interactive primer that anyone can use. It's built on curated Google sources covering the quantum era, quantum computing breakthroughs like Willow, Quantum Echoes, and surface code error suppression, industry PQC standards, Google's own deployments, and the latest research.

In the Gemini Notebook, you can:

  • Get answers grounded in Google's sources.

  • Listen to a podcast-style audio overview.

  • Test your PQC knowledge with flashcards.

  • Explore an interactive visual diagram of the quantum threat.

  • Read a concise briefing document.

Try these prompts

To get started, here are a few questions to ask the notebook:

  • For CISOs: "What should a CISO prioritize in the first 90 days of a PQC migration?"

  • For anyone new to PQC: "Explain store-now-decrypt-later in plain terms."

  • For developers: "How does hybrid ML-KEM key exchange work in Chrome?"

As with all generative AI, the notebook can make mistakes, so check its responses against the linked sources.

What's at stake

Previous cryptographic migrations, such as moving from SHA-1 or upgrading TLS, have taken a decade or more. Waiting for the availability of a cryptographically-relevant quantum computer before beginning the migration journey represents a significant security risk given the importance of public-key cryptography for securing digital essentials like web traffic, software updates, digital identities, and signatures.

For CISOs, we recommend that you start by:

  • Understanding where vulnerable cryptography lives in your organization.

  • Identifying and prioritizing data and systems most at risk from quantum threats, and developing a plan for addressing these risks.

  • Anticipate system-wide effects that PQC migration could have.

  • Building crypto-agility into your security plans, using learnings from past experiences like Heartbleed.

Additional detail on these recommendations is available in our previous blog post.  

For the broader security community, the transition only succeeds if this knowledge is accessible to everyone — not just organizations with dedicated cryptography teams.

How Google is putting PQC into practice

We’ve been deploying PQC for years. Highlights include:

  • Hybrid Kyber/ML-KEM key exchange protecting Chrome traffic

  • PQC in Android

  • Quantum-safe digital signatures in Cloud KMS

  • PQC for Google's internal communications

We also co-founded the Post-Quantum Cryptography Alliance at the Linux Foundation with industry leaders including Amazon Web Services, Cisco, IBM, and NVIDIA to support open-source tools like Open Quantum Safe.

Build a PQC notebook for your own team

Here’s how you can create a resource similar to our PQC Gemini Notebook, specific to your organization’s needs:

  • Curate trusted sources. Start with a focused set of authoritative research, standards, and guidance.

  • Write neutral prompts. Keep instructions factual so outputs stay grounded in your sources.

  • Add AI disclaimers and a welcome note. Tell readers what the notebook covers and remind them that AI can make mistakes.

  • Review all output with human oversight. Have experts check every artifact before you share it.

Start preparing today

The quantum transition has already started, but preparing your organization doesn't have to begin with a 100-page whitepaper. Start by understanding the threat, then assess your cryptographic inventory and build a migration roadmap.

You can get started with the Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography Gemini Notebook and share it with your team today. To learn more about Google Cloud’s approach to PQC, check out our dedicated Google Cloud PQC Resource Hub.

entries.content:
Praveen Kumar

Customer Engineer, Data & AI

The reality for most organizations is that data lives everywhere. As engineering teams expand and adopt specialized platforms for their workloads, enterprise data naturally disperses across multiple clouds and operational systems. When analytical and AI initiatives require context from across the entire organization,these teams traditionally face a difficult trade-off: build complex extraction pipelines to copy data into a central repository or accept fragmented reporting.

Traditional architectures address this fragmentation with scheduled extraction pipelines that copy remote datasets into a central staging warehouse. This approach creates synchronization lag, adds recurring storage costs, and triggers variable network egress fees. When schemas change upstream, pipelines break, and teams spend hours reconciling metrics across out-of-sync dashboards.

BigQuery and Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse offer a streamlined way to solve this challenge with a foundation based on the open Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification. Rather than moving data to the compute engine, you can bring Google Cloud compute and generative AI directly to your data, querying it in place across Databricks, Snowflake, and AWS Glue.

In this post, we walk through how to configure Databricks Unity Catalog for federation into BigQuery (AWS Glue and Snowflake set up in appendix), run a single query joining data across all three external catalogs, and use conversational analytics in BigQuery to explore the consolidated data with natural language.

Figure 1: BigQuery federates metadata across external Apache Iceberg REST catalogs through Lakehouse, enabling in-place conversational analytics without data migration.

The borderless lakehouse architecture

This solution uses Lakehouse runtime catalog to synchronize metadata from other cloud providers, allowing you to query data with BigQuery or external open source engines through the Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint, all without migrating the data. Because Databricks Unity Catalog, Snowflake Horizon Catalog, and AWS Glue Data Catalog support the open Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification, you can apply a consistent connection pattern across all three platforms.

When you run a federated query, Lakehouse runtime catalog separates metadata synchronization from storage access:

  • Metadata synchronization: Lakehouse runtime catalog periodically syncs schemas, snapshot pointers, and table definitions from the remote catalog based on a refresh schedule you define.

  • Direct storage access: During query runtime, a compatible engine reads Parquet data files directly from remote object storage, such as Amazon S3, using temporary credentials issued by the remote platform.

All query processing runs within Google cloud compute such as BigQuery or Managed Service  for Apache Spark. Remote Databricks clusters, Snowflake virtual warehouses, and AWS compute instances are not invoked during execution.

Authentication follows an explicit three-step deployment pattern: create the federated catalog in Google Cloud, inspect its configuration to retrieve its automatically generated service account, and grant access permissions within the remote platform.

You can use AI to generate sample data. The schema details for tables are provided below.

Configure Databricks Unity Catalog

We begin in Databricks by preparing the catalog and table. In Unity Catalog, federated access requires that your target schema be associated with an external location registered in Databricks:

Go to Databricks Admin account and under User Management, create a Databricks Service Principal and make a note of its UUID

command-line tool. You will need your Databricks workspace URL and the application ID of your Databricks service principal:

Return to Databricks to assign permissions to your service principal:

You must grant the 

EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA
privilege to the Databricks Service Principal on the target schemas or catalog to enable credential vending for external data access.

Finally, to complete the connection, configure the federation policy on the Databricks service principal with the following details -

  • Issuer URL* -  https://accounts.google.com

  • Subject* - numeric subject ID returned by the catalog describe command eg 1124251400450xxxxxxxx

  • Audiences - https://accounts.cloud.databricks.com

Run one query across three clouds

In our environment, sales transactions reside natively in BigQuery:

BigQuery processes the joins in place. Notice that Snowflake identifiers appear in uppercase (

CORE.DIM_CUSTOMERS
), while Databricks and AWS Glue maintain lowercase table paths.

Figure 2 - Query results combining data across Snowflake, Databricks, and AWS Glue.

Explore cross-cloud data with natural language

Because federated Iceberg tables behave like native tables within BigQuery, downstream analytical features inherit access directly. You can point conversational analytics in BigQuery at these federated schemas to let team members explore cross-cloud data using natural language prompts.

To give conversational analytics full operational context, we save our federated join as a logical view:

Analyze sales performance in natural language

When you ask conversational analytics in BigQuery:

"Who are our top customers by total sales revenue, what products did they buy, and which stores did they shop at?"

Conversational analytics evaluates the schema across all three remote catalogs, generates the SQL statement, executes the query, and presents the response.

Figure 3: Conversational analytics in BigQuery translates plain-language prompts into federated queries across Snowflake, Databricks, and AWS Glue.

Plan for caching and data residency

Before deploying federated catalogs in production, consider these operational behaviors:

  • Background refresh timing: The 

    --refresh-interval
    flag controls metadata synchronization. The minimum interval is 300 seconds. For larger catalogs containing hundreds of tables, metadata retrieval can take longer. If a sync cycle overruns, BigQuery skips the next scheduled run to avoid task queuing.

  • Automatic query caching: BigQuery caches retrieved cross-cloud data blocks in the region where your federated catalog resides (e.g. 

    us-central1
    ). This helps reduce network transfer on repeated queries. Because cached blocks reside within Google Cloud storage in that region, confirm that this aligns with your organization's data residency policies.

  • Encryption controls: Cross-cloud cache blocks use Google-managed encryption keys. If your organization enforces the 

    constraints/gcp.restrictNonCmekServices
    policy constraint, BigQuery bypasses the cache and reads directly from remote storage for every query.

  • Monitoring access metrics: You can evaluate cache utilization in your query execution plans. Check the 

    objectStorageStats
    section in BigQuery job statistics to compare 
    cacheBytesRead
    against 
    objectStorageBytesRead
    .

Next steps

In summary, Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse helps you activate your data regardless of where it lives without costly migrations or building additional data pipelines.   Get started today by reviewing the borderless Lakehouse architecture documentation to learn more about supported regions and credential configurations. You can work through the borderless Lakehouse codelab to practice federating external catalogs step-by-step. Finally, connect with your Google Cloud account team or customer engineer to evaluate borderless lakehouse patterns for your specific data platforms or industries.

entries.title: Gemini 4 Argon available on Google Cloud, built to help solve your business’ hardest problems
entries.summary: Last week we announced that Gemini Enterprise has evolved to make it even simpler to get work done, and introduced the Gemini agent, your new universal agent for work. It's always on and ready to answer your questions. It will write code, complete longer and more complex tasks, or perform whatever you need to get the job done, all from a single prompt box. And model intelligence underpins it all.
entries.content:
Michael Gerstenhaber

VP, Product Management, Gemini, Google Cloud

Last week we announced that Gemini Enterprise has evolved to make it even simpler to get work done, and introduced the Gemini agent, your new universal agent for work. It's always on and ready to answer your questions. It will write code, complete longer and more complex tasks, or perform whatever you need to get the job done, all from a single prompt box. And model intelligence underpins it all.

To enable a new frontier of work, we are making our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, available on Google Cloud. 

We trained Argon to work with both depth and precision, which allows it to maintain context across long, multi-step tasks which are reinforced with strong domain expertise along the way. Whether your team is running complex software builds, handling detailed financial and legal work, or deploying cybersecurity tools like CodeMender, Argon helps your teams maintain focus from start to finish. 

Customers and partners using Gemini 4 Argon

Four ways Argon changes how your business works

1. Hand off your hardest work

Your teams already use Gemini for business to answer questions and draft content. With Argon, they can hand off the deep, multi-step work that used to take hours or days, and get back finished work they can use.

Argon reads long documents that mix text, tables, charts and images, and turns them into one clear output grounded in those sources. It can pull findings from many sources into a single structured answer, analyze data over time, and write stronger legal, finance, and executive documents. On long tasks, it keeps going until the job is done. We trained Argon to respect system boundaries, report negative findings honestly, and pause for confirmation before taking irreversible steps, and it tells you when it couldn't find something or finish a task.

Customers who tested Argon tell us it excels at turning huge, unstructured inputs into cohesive outputs.

"As software development becomes more agentic, teams need models that can support long-running, multi-step work across all stages of the development lifecycle. Gemini 4 Argon is designed to help organizations bring AI into development, security, and operations while keeping it within established enterprise workflows and controls.” – Stuart Moncada, VP, GitLab.

2. Precise, verifiable results on the work that drives your business

entries.content:
Karl Weinmeister

Director, Developer Relations

When we talk about agents, that doesn't necessarily mean we're talking about Python. In today's modern ecosystem, an agent might run as a high-concurrency Go microservice on Cloud Run, or live inside a browser tab calling Chrome's on-device model. Yet many agent frameworks assume a Python-only stack. That assumption forces teams to either spin up a Python service just for their agent workloads, or to build agent orchestration logic from scratch in their own language.

Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) removes that trade-off with coverage for Python, Go, TypeScript, Java, and Kotlin. Each version of the ADK is built from the ground up for its own runtime and type system, while sharing a unified architecture with interoperability through open protocols.

A shared foundation

Picking a language doesn't lock in your architecture: all five support the same open protocols. ADK includes a Model Context Protocol client in every language, so a custom tool exposed as an MCP server can be called from any of them immediately.

For multi-agent systems, ADK supports the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, allowing an agent to communicate with a remote agent over HTTP. Through A2A, agents written in different languages or frameworks are interoperable.

Starting agent-first

To get started, run the one-time setup command to check your Google Cloud authentication, install the CLI, and then set up first-party ADK skills in coding agents like Antigravity, Claude Code, or Codex:

Then, run the scaffold command to generate a working project with A2A endpoints and deployment config for Cloud Run, Gemini Enterprise Agent Runtime, or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE):

Both the ADK for Python and ADK for Kotlin repositories also ship agent builder skills in their source trees, and the 

adk.dev/llms.txt
resource gives any coding agent on-demand API documentation across all five languages.

Coding-agent skills scaffold your project while MCP and A2A connect all five language runtimes.

Hands-on view of each ADK

The clearest way to feel the difference between the five languages is to define the same weather tool in each one and see how its design fits the runtime.

Python

In ADK for Python, you don't need a decorator or a schema builder class. You pass a plain Python function into the 

tools
parameter, and ADK inspects its signature, type hints, and docstring at startup to automatically construct the tool declaration and Pydantic parameter schema:

Beyond fast prototyping, Python is ADK's reference implementation, shipping the broadest set of Google Cloud integrations (BigQuery, Spanner, Bigtable) and model adapters (Gemini, Anthropic, OpenAI, LiteLLM). Paired with the 

adk eval
or 
agents-cli eval run
commands, its evaluation tooling scores agent trajectories against golden datasets in continuous integration (CI) to test the whole system end to end, even when your production service runs in another language.

Go

While Python leads in experimentation and evaluation, ADK for Go hits the sweet spot for production backend engineering.

A Go tool function takes the 

agent.Context
configuration and a strongly typed input struct. The 
functiontool.New
 function uses Go generics to infer both the input and output schemas from your 

struct
tags:

Because the 

functiontool.New
function is generic over your handler's signature, the Go compiler verifies that your function matches the expected contract before your binary ever runs.

Go was also the first language after Python to ship the ADK 2.0 Graph Workflow runtime. When you need deterministic control flow alongside LLM reasoning, the 

workflow.New
function wires agents and plain Go functions into a directed graph with conditional routing and parallel steps:

Where Go really stands out is in production on Cloud Run and GKE. A compiled Go agent packages onto a roughly 2 MiB Google distroless static base image, with no language VM or heavy dependency tree. A static Go binary binds to its port as soon as the container starts, skipping the module imports of dynamic languages and the JAR unpacking and JIT warmup of JVM services.

After it's running, Go's concurrency model fits agent workloads naturally. Each goroutine starts with a 2 KB stack and minimal scheduling overhead, so a single instance can multiplex thousands of concurrent streaming requests and tool calls. ADK for Go also includes built-in A2A server handlers and OpenTelemetry tracing out of the box.

TypeScript

TypeScript erases type annotations when compiling to JavaScript, so runtime reflection isn't an option. Instead, ADK for TypeScript pairs with Zod. You pass a 

z.object(...)
schema to the 
FunctionTool
function, and TypeScript statically infers the parameter types of your 
execute
callback from that single declaration:

Your runtime input validation, the JSON Schema sent to the model, and your IDE autocomplete inside the 

execute
callback all flow from one source of truth.

TypeScript also runs on the ADK 2.0 Graph Workflow engine and ships a standalone browser bundle. Beyond Node.js services, you can run an ADK agent directly in a browser tab using WebMCP for page-level tools and Chrome's on-device Prompt API.

Java

ADK for Java snaps right in for teams who have standardized on Maven, Gradle, and Spring Boot. You add 

@Schema
annotations to method parameters and assemble agents by using a fluent 
LlmAgent.builder()
API:

At runtime, the runner streams agent events reactively through RxJava. For local testing and existing JVM apps, ADK for Java ships a Maven Dev UI plugin alongside first-party bridges for Spring AI and LangChain4j.

Kotlin

ADK for Kotlin takes a strong stance on build-time safety. Its Kotlin Symbol Processing (KSP) compiler plugin reads 

@Tool
and 
@Param
annotations at build time and emits the tool schema directly into bytecode:

If a tool signature uses an unsupported type or declares a default value on a non-nullable parameter, your Gradle build fails immediately instead of breaking in production. Because the 

.generatedTools()
function uses zero runtime reflection, it survives Android R8 shrinking.

That zero-reflection design makes it possible to run the entire agent loop locally on Android. It offers JVM server support, including a Spring AI bridge and experimental ADK 2.0 graph workflows. On-device, ADK for Kotlin integrates with LiteRT-LM for tool calling and ML Kit (Gemini Nano) for text generation. It also works with Room and AppSearch for local state, and Android AppFunctions for OS-level actions, all without requiring a network connection.

Choice without compromise

Having five native languages in ADK means you don't have to pick a single runtime for your entire organization. Because every version of ADK speaks MCP and A2A, each component of your system can use the language that fits it best.

What languages have you used to build agents with Google's ADK? Let me know what stack you're running on X, LinkedIn, or Bluesky.

entries.content:
Jeff Nelson

Developer Relations Engineer, Google

Imagine your compliance team notices that payments are taking longer than expected to clear. They suspect fraud, and you’re the data scientist helping figure out which transactions to investigate first. Assembling that shortlist requires ingesting and cleaning raw transaction logs, training a model on past fraud, scoring new records, and scheduling the pipeline to run daily. Here’s how you can build that workflow end to end with an agent, using the Data Agent Kit inside the Antigravity IDE.

Introducing the Data Agent Kit

Data Agent Kit helps you work with Google Cloud data through a plugin for coding agents or an extension for Visual Studio Code-based IDEs. It brings two significant additions to the workflow:

  • Help for your agent: MCP tools connect your agent to data services. Skills are Markdown files that give it instructions and best practices for working with your data stack

  • Tools in your IDE: work with Google’s Agentic Data Cloud, from querying databases to deploying an Airflow pipeline, without leaving your editor

Loading the data

Let’s start with the raw transaction logs in Google Cloud Storage. You can ask the agent to create a notebook that loads them into BigQuery using Spark:

The agent generates a Jupyter notebook that loads the JSON logs into a BigQuery table named raw_transactions. You can open the notebook, review the code, and run it using a preconfigured Spark Serverless runtime from the IDE.

Running a generated PySpark notebook

After the notebook runs, you can open the raw_transactions table with the Data Agent Kit. The extension allows you to browse the table and inspect its metadata right from the IDE.

Inspecting a BigQuery table in the IDE

The records are now in BigQuery, but they aren’t ready for model training yet. First, we’ll handle duplicate and incomplete records, then join the remaining records with info about who sent and received each payment.

Cleaning it up

Let’s put the cleanup logic into a dbt project so we can run it on each new batch of data. We’ll also test that each transaction appears only once. Prompt the agent:

The agent generates a dbt project with SQL models for cleaning and enriching the data. Take a look at the generated code to check how it handles duplicates and joins reference tables. Then run dbt build in the terminal. This builds the staging and enriched tables in BigQuery, along with a separate table for records with missing transaction IDs. dbt also runs the uniqueness test.

Validating dbt models in the integrated terminal

We also keep the is_fraud column, which indicates whether a past transaction was fraudulent. We’ll train the model on records with known labels and use it to score new transactions, where we’re unsure yet whether fraud occurred.

Building the review queue

With the data prepared, let’s ask the agent to create a training notebook using a Random Forest classifier running on Spark Serverless.

Review and run the notebook, then check its evaluation output to see how well the model separates fraudulent transactions from legitimate ones. You can also use the Data Agent Kit extension to verify that the trained model artifacts were saved to Google Cloud Storage.

Verifying the trained model artifacts in Google Cloud Storage

Now we can use the saved model to score transactions that don’t have an is_fraud value yet:

In this example, the inference notebook scores the unlabeled transactions in BigQuery and sends those with an estimated fraud probability of 50% or higher to the Spanner review queue. The flagged records help the team decide where to investigate, but they still need to determine whether fraud occurred.

Look at how the inference notebook filters and writes flagged records, then run it. Once it finishes, query the Spanner table in the IDE to inspect the results.

Querying flagged transactions in the Spanner table

This table is the list we set out to build. The compliance team can now start reviewing transactions, and we have a workflow that gets records from raw logs into the queue.

So far, we have been kicking off each step ourselves. We can now connect them so the workflow runs automatically each day.

Running it again tomorrow

Each day we will load the latest logs, apply the dbt transformations, and score unlabeled transactions using the saved model. We’ll use the Managed Service for Apache Airflow to run these steps in order. Ask the agent: 

The agent generates a YAML pipeline definition and deployment configuration. The pipeline definition sets the schedule and dependencies between steps. Meanwhile, the deployment configuration specifies the Airflow environment where it will run.

Data Agent Kit then turns the definition into an Airflow DAG, which you can explore as an interactive graph in the IDE. Open the pipeline under “Orchestration Pipelines” and click a task to inspect it. For notebook tasks, you can follow the link straight back to the code.

Inspecting a data pipeline

With the Airflow environment configured, click “Run pipeline” in the canvas. Data Agent Kit packages the notebooks and dbt project, deploys the DAG, and triggers a run. Open the pipeline’s execution history to follow its progress. You can also select individual tasks to inspect their status, duration, and logs.

Kicking off an Airflow DAG and inspecting the logs

Airflow will run the pipeline every day, taking new batches of data from raw logs to the review queue. The compliance team can now focus on flagged transactions, and you’ve automated the work of getting those records to them!

Try it yourself

If you are ready to try this for yourself, we have designed a codelab that walks you through the full setup so you can build and run this workflow. You can also read our documentation or check out the skills and tools in the open-source repository on GitHub.

entries.content:
Betsy Beyer

SRE Program Manager

David Huska

Software Engineer, Site Reliability Engineer

How Google runs production systems, rewritten for the modern cloud and AI era

A decade ago, Google released Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems with O'Reilly Media. What began as a collection of our practices for managing large-scale infrastructure became a bestselling book, and inspired many organizations to adopt the reliability practices it outlined: applying software engineering to operations to build systems that are scalable, reliable, and sustainable.

Over the past ten years, computing landscapes have undergone profound shifts. AI, microservices, multi-cloud deployments, serverless paradigms, and platform engineering have all reshaped how we build and operate software. To mark the 10th anniversary of the book's release, we are excited to announce the completely rewritten second edition of the Google SRE book, reflecting a decade of lessons learned both inside Google and across the broader industry, to offer fresh guidance tailored for today's operational challenges.

Why update the book?

When we published the first edition, many organizations were focused on early cloud migrations and just starting to transition from monolithic architectures. Today, with organizations delivering software at a high velocity and at global scale, the challenge is no longer adopting cloud infrastructure, but maintaining high reliability in the face of the immense complexity.

Modern production environments operate under constant change. System boundaries are more complex, dependencies are deep, and failure modes are more complex and damaging than ever before. The explosion of resource-intensive workloads like generative AI has changed the economics and operational requirements of infrastructure management.

Writing this second edition required us to take a step back and evaluate what it takes to successfully implement SRE today.

A decade of evolution: How SRE practices have progressed

The second edition takes a deep dive into how foundational site reliability engineering practices have matured over the last ten years, shifting from manual, task-specific work toward automated, platform-wide capabilities. Consider, for example:

SLOs and error budgets: In 2016, teams relied on basic availability metrics and manual error budget policies. Today, practices have matured into user-centric, multi-tiered SLOs with dynamic burn-rate alerting and automated policy enforcement.

Monitoring and observability: Early setups centered on static dashboards, basic logs, and manual alert triage. Modern observability leverages OpenTelemetry, distributed tracing, and automated anomaly correlation to find root causes quickly.

Automation and platforms: Operations have shifted from writing custom scripts for isolated tasks to using declarative infrastructure as code, internal developer platforms, and resilient, self-healing systems.

Reliability testing: Rather than relying solely on scheduled game days and synthetic load tests, modern engineering embeds continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing, and live production canary verification.

Capacity and resource management: Manual provisioning and static forecasting have been replaced by dynamic auto-scaling, cloud FinOps alignment, and dedicated cost and cluster optimization for GPU and TPU workloads.

Organizational models: SRE has expanded beyond dedicated teams assigned to specific applications. Today's organizations use hybrid models, platform engineering integrations, and reliability champions embedded across product teams.

SRE in the age of AI

Then there’s the dual relationship between SRE and artificial Intelligence: how SRE supports AI infrastructure, and how SRE teams use AI to enhance operational reliability.

Running large language models (LLMs) and foundation models introduces novel reliability challenges. The book outlines methodologies for operating AI infrastructure at scale:

  • Managing massive GPU and TPU hardware cluster reliability and network topologies
  • Monitoring non-deterministic outputs and latency characteristics unique to AI
  • Ensuring pipeline reliability for continuous model training, fine-tuning, and data processing

AI is also rapidly becoming a force multiplier for reliability engineers. The second edition shares practical frameworks for enhancing human operational efficiency:

  • Using generative AI tools to assist in real-time incident triage and postmortem generation
  • Interrogating complex system telemetry using natural language queries
  • Using predictive machine learning models to identify resource bottlenecks before outages occur

What hasn’t changed? The importance of culture

While technologies and architectures continuously evolve, the core principles of SRE remain intact, and are key to establishing a reliability-focused culture. Accordingly, the second edition re-emphasizes and expands upon the human elements of system engineering, and how to get there.

Whether you’re new to the field, a practitioner, an engineering manager, or a technology executive, the rewritten second edition of Site Reliability Engineering serves as your definitive roadmap for the next era of production systems.

You can order your copy today in physical format (see Google Books) or digital format from O'Reilly.

As a business intelligence user, this probably sounds familiar: Most dashboards only provide you with a standardized canvas and a fixed library of charts, and the “analysis” consists of a CSV export that takes you to another system. Or sometimes it's designing the dashboard that’s the challenge: You can picture the executive briefing, the customer-facing portal, or the interactive explainer that you want, but can’t assemble it out of the available grid tiles.

Either way, the solution has always been to build a custom application. The advent of AI has sped up the process — a working prototype now takes an afternoon — but the excitement of that first demo fades fast. Without access to governed data, row-level security, an infrastructure owner, or a clear path through security review, a tool written by an LLM is simply a prototype that can never go to production.

Today, to bridge this gap, we are announcing Looker Data Apps (in preview) — pairing the speed of agent-generated applications with the governance, security, and trust of your existing Looker governance framework. Describe what you need in plain language, and the agent builds it as a real, production-grade application hosted natively inside Looker!

What is a data app?

A data app is a bespoke, interactive web application generated by an AI agent and hosted natively within Looker. While dashboards provide top-down visibility, data apps serve as an active system of action designed around a specific operational workflow. A data app:

  • Goes beyond standard grid tiles with pixel-perfect, bespoke layouts configured for a specific operational role or job-to-be-done.

  • Enables business users to input parameters, test scenarios, run live simulations, and update underlying records.

  • Connects end-to-end business processes by connecting data analysis to business execution tasks like updating source records or dispatching events to tools like Salesforce and Jira.

Build pixel-perfect interfaces using AI developer tools like Claude Code or Antigravity CLI, grounded directly by Looker’s semantic layer.

Expanding your semantic layer into an application platform

Data apps do not replace dashboards; they expand the boundaries of what you can build on top of your existing dashboards and semantic layer.

  • Dashboards excel at aggregate visibility and passive reporting. Data apps handle active execution, letting users modify parameters and trigger downstream business tasks.

  • Dashboards provide consistency using standardized chart libraries. Data apps deliver broad flexibility, unlocking custom web components and specialized interactions.

  • Data apps are grounded in governed data to ensure accuracy. Whether users are reviewing a KPI dashboard or adjusting budgets in a data app, all logic is governed centrally with the LookML semantic layer to eliminate metric discrepancies and hallucinations.

Transform analysis into action with customizable, multi-page web app experiences and embedded operational workflows.

Built for enterprise scale

We designed Looker Data Apps for demanding, governed enterprises.

  • Every measure is grounded in the semantic layer. Every app you build directly inherits your existing semantic models, row-level security, and access controls. Calculations stay consistent across the enterprise, and built-in query inspection lets teams audit every line of generated SQL to eliminate metric hallucinations.

  • Zero-code by default. Deploy agent-generated React applications directly inside Looker with no code. Or users can use LLMs like Claude Code and Antigravity CLI to build interactive apps and deploy them as data apps in minutes.

  • No runtime token costs. LLM tokens are only consumed when you’re designing or generating the app. After that, every end-user interaction runs on native Looker APIs and models. Put a data app in front of 50 people or 5,000 and the marginal cost doesn't change.

  • As easy as embedding a dashboard. You can deploy your data apps into external portals using the same workflows you use to embed a dashboard. No new pipelines, no custom application code, no second permission models.

From prototype to production in minutes

The days of having to choose between basic dashboards and investing valuable engineering time to build bespoke systems are coming to an end. Instead of letting prototypes stall in sandboxes due to compliance and security barriers, Looker Data Apps allows teams to deploy governed, production-grade tools in minutes.

Looker Data Apps are now in preview. Get started today.

entries.content:
Haiyang Qi

Software Engineer

Haoming Chen

Engineering Manager

Overview

Since introducing zero-shot time-series forecasting in BigQuery with AI.FORECAST — initially powered by TimesFM 2.0 and later upgraded to TimesFM 2.5 — you have been able to generate forecasts directly in SQL without training or managing custom models. However, up until TimesFM 2.5, these foundation models were limited to univariate forecasting, predicting future values from the history of a single time series alone. In practice, most real-world forecasting problems are multivariate, where related targets and external drivers like weather, promotions, and holidays jointly shape future outcomes.

Today, we are thrilled to announce the preview of TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery. Developed by Google Research, TimesFM 3.0 is a 330-million parameter state-of-the-art foundation model designed to unlock native multivariate time-series forecasting directly inside BigQuery SQL. TimesFM 3.0 ranks #1 across all three major public time-series leaderboards — GIFT-Eval, FEV-Bench, and TIME — achieving top zero-shot accuracy on both covariate and multivariate forecasting tasks compared to existing foundation models.

Alongside its new multivariate capabilities, TimesFM 3.0 also serves as a drop-in upgrade for univariate forecasting via AI.FORECAST and anomaly detection via AI.DETECT_ANOMALIES. Existing workflows can immediately benefit from higher benchmark accuracy simply by specifying model => 'TimesFM 3.0'.

What’s new: Multivariate foundation modeling

With TimesFM 3.0, BigQuery brings enterprise-grade multivariate modeling into familiar SQL workflows via AI.FORECAST:

Multivariate forecasting with BigQuery SQL

To see how these capabilities work together, let’s forecast daily commuter (subscriber_trips) and leisure (casual_trips) bike rides over a seven-day horizon using the NYC Citi Bike public dataset (bigquery-public-data.new_york.citibike_trips).

BigQuery uses a single-table input format for multivariate forecasting that combines two sets of rows:

  • Historical observation rows: timestamps between start time (2016-01-01) and the forecast cutoff date (2016-06-01), fully populated with target metrics, past covariates, and known future covariates

  • Future horizon rows: timestamps across the seven-day forecast horizon (2016-06-01 to 2016-06-07) populated with known future covariates, while target columns and past-only covariates are set to NULL

This query highlights the three multivariate dimensions supported in TimesFM 3.0:

  • Forecasting correlated targets (target_cols) Instead of running separate models for each rider segment, passing TARGET_COLS => ['subscriber_trips', 'casual_trips'] forecasts both metrics jointly in a single call. TimesFM 3.0 captures the cross-series dynamics between commuter and casual riders — such as shared weather sensitivity and diverging weekend ridership patterns.

  • Using past covariates (past_covariate_cols) Some signals can only be observed historically and are not known in advance, such as average ride duration (avg_duration_min), historical foot traffic, or unplanned service disruptions. Passing PAST_COVARIATE_COLS => ['avg_duration_min'] (with future horizon rows set to NULL) gives the model historical context to distinguish temporary shocks from underlying trends without requiring future values for that feature.

  • Using future covariates (future_covariate_cols) Other external drivers are known ahead of time across both the historical window and the forecast horizon — such as weekends (is_weekend), holidays, or scheduled promotions. Passing FUTURE_COVARIATE_COLS => ['is_weekend'] (populated across all rows through 2016-06-07) allows TimesFM 3.0 to condition its seven-day predictions directly on upcoming calendar events.

Understanding the output

The function returns structured predictions for each target column specified in target_cols. For each column in target_cols, AI.FORECAST returns a struct containing the point forecast (value) and the lower and upper prediction interval bounds:

TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery Conversational Analytics

You can also run multivariate forecasts using natural language in BigQuery Conversational Analytics. On the same bigquery-public-data.new_york.citibike_trips dataset, you can simply ask "Forecast both daily subscriber and casual trips for June 1–7, 2016 using two month historical data, with average trip duration as a past covariate and weekend indicator as a future covariate." Conversational Analytics automatically generates and executes the underlying AI.FORECAST query with TimesFM 3.0, returning a summary of the results, interactive forecast charts with prediction intervals for each target, and key forecast insights.

Multivariate forecasting with TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery Conversational Analytics, generating 7-day predictions, interactive charts, and insights from a natural-language prompt.

Summary and next steps

With native multivariate support in TimesFM 3.0, BigQuery brings state-of-the-art foundation model forecasting to complex, interconnected enterprise datasets without requiring data movement, custom feature engineering pipelines, or dedicated model hosting infrastructure.

To start forecasting with TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery:

  • Read the Google Research blog post to learn more about the TimesFM 3.0 model architecture and capabilities.

  • Explore the BigQuery TimesFM documentation.

  • Follow the step-by-step multivariate forecasting tutorial.

  • Try AI.FORECAST with `model => 'TimesFM 3.0'` directly in the BigQuery Studio SQL workspace.

  • Try AI.DETECT_ANOMALIES with `model => 'TimesFM 3.0'` for univariate time series anomaly detection in BigQuery.

  • Try AI.EVALUATE with `model => 'TimesFM 3.0'` for univariate time series evaluation in BigQuery.

The Google Cloud Data Analytics, BI, and Database teams

Recent product news and updates from our data analytics, database and business intelligence teams.

October 5 - October 9

  • Data Agent Kit is now generally available to bring Google Data Cloud to any coding agent

    Data Agent Kit provides a free collection of Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and Google-authored agent skills that connect more than 15 Google Data Cloud services directly to coding agents across VS Code, Antigravity, Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex. This release expands support for developers and data practitioners to inspect schemas, author queries, and build end-to-end data pipelines in natural language directly from their IDE or CLI. Read the announcement blog.

  • Spanner Omni is now generally available for deploy-anywhere, multi-model workloads

    Spanner Omni brings Spanner's distributed SQL, graph, vector, and key-value capabilities to any environment, including on-premises data centers, other public clouds via Kubernetes or VMs, and local developer laptops. Organizations can build and run multi-model applications with consistent APIs and query engines across hybrid and multi-cloud footprints while seamlessly scaling to managed Spanner on Google Cloud. Read the launch blog and explore how Spanner also removed cumulative mutation limits for DML transactions.

  • AlloyDB delivers PostgreSQL for agents and native BM25 hybrid search

    We announced PostgreSQL for agents in AlloyDB, introducing an agentic database architecture engineered for real-time data access at agent scale with workload isolation. In addition, native BM25 ranking is now in Preview for AlloyDB and Cloud SQL, allowing developers to combine keyword search and vector embeddings directly in PostgreSQL without maintaining an external search engine. For hybrid deployments, the AlloyDB Omni RPM Orchestrator is now generally available, and you can dive deeper in our new Build AI apps and agents with AlloyDB eBook.

  • Lakehouse runtime catalog adds regional endpoints across 22 regions and GA support for flexible column names

    Lakehouse runtime catalog regional endpoints are now live across 22 Google Cloud regions across the Americas, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East, supporting both the Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint and the Apache Hive catalog endpoint to help customers meet strict data residency and sovereignty requirements. In addition, flexible column names for Apache Iceberg tables are now generally available by default across Iceberg external tables and managed tables, enabling seamless querying of columns containing spaces, hyphens, and Unicode characters. We also announced the Preview of cross-cloud caching and connections for the borderless Lakehouse.

  • Unlock predictive and agent-ready insights with BigQuery augmented analytics TVFs, TabFM, and identity columns

    BigQuery introduced augmented analytics table-valued functions (TVFs): six built-in functions that automate metric diagnostics, trend analysis, and pattern discovery directly where your data lives and integrate as skills for AI agents. We also introduced TabFM in BigQuery to bring tabular foundation model capabilities to predictive analytics, alongside BigQuery identity columns to automatically generate sequential surrogate keys and simplify data warehouse pipelines.

  • Dataflow adds Pause/Resume and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU support for large-scale AI workloads

    New Dataflow capabilities make it easier to run high-throughput streaming and batch AI pipelines at scale, including Pause/Resume job controls and support for NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs. And for teams running Apache Spark workloads, learn how to mitigate compute stockouts and maximize availability using flexible VMs.

  • Unlock up to 3x higher QPS and microsecond latency with Memorystore for Valkey 9.1

    Memorystore for Valkey 9.1 is now available, delivering up to 3x higher queries per second (QPS) and microsecond-level caching latencies to accelerate high-throughput applications and real-time AI agent state management. Read the blog.

  • Customer momentum across Google Data Cloud — Yahoo, PayPal, Surescripts, Airwallex, and Lucius AI

    Organizations across industries are scaling their data and AI foundations on Google Data Cloud. Yahoo uses flexible VMs in Managed Service for Apache Spark to reduce provisioning failures by 85%, while PayPal migrated mission-critical analytics workloads to Managed Service for Apache Spark to scale and reduce operational overhead. On the database front, Surescripts migrated 30.5 billion annual healthcare transactions to AlloyDB with 99.998% uptime, Airwallex manages more than 5,000 databases with 99.99% availability on Cloud SQL with a team of four DBAs, and Lucius AI runs a 210,000-tender global platform on AlloyDB and MCP with 47x faster ScaNN vector search.

September 7 - September 10

  • Pub/Sub SMTs can now AI Inference your Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform models!

    Pub/Sub AI Inference SMTs allow you to apply inference on an incoming stream of events using models hosted in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. The model’s prediction is appended to your event, making it available for downstream processing in your data warehouse (like BigQuery) or operational database (like BigTable). This feature, now generally available, can dramatically simplify or enhance anomaly detection systems you are operating. 

  • PostgreSQL Source Connector is now generally available in Managed Service for Apache Kafka!

    Managed Service for Apache Kafka’s PostgreSQL connector allows customers to capture changes from their PostgreSQL database and ingest them into their Kafka infrastructure with low latency. This source connector is compatible withCloud SQL for Postgres, AlloyDB, and self-managed PostgreSQL databases. Try this along with our entire portfolio of managed connectors, including MirrorMaker 2.0, BigQuery, Cloud Storage, and Pub/Sub! E-mail kafka-hotline@google.com if you have questions or feedback!

  • Pause-on-failure for Dataflow batch jobs is GA

    Dataflow pause-on-failure enables you to preserve the state of a batch Dataflow job before it fails. By pausing your Dataflow job, you can address issues that are external to the pipeline and resume processing without losing completed work. This helps you better manage resource costs and improve job reliability when you face temporary outages or capacity constraints.

  • The insertAll API is now the BigQuery Storage Write API (REST)

    The legacy insertAll streaming API is now rebranded as the BigQuery Storage Write API (REST). By dropping the "legacy" label, developers can confidently build long-term HTTP-based streaming workflows. This stateless JSON-over-HTTPS endpoint offers a lightweight alternative to heavy gRPC libraries—ideal for serverless web apps, IoT telemetry, and AI logging. The transition is seamless for existing users, requiring zero code changes and offering 100% backward compatibility. However, the Storage Write API (gRPC) version remains the recommended standard for high-throughput, continuous pipelines.

August 31 - September 4

  • Stateful processing is available in BigQuery continuous queries in Preview

    Stateful operations significantly expand what’s possible with BigQuery continuous queries. This feature allows users to leverage functions like 
    JOIN
    s, aggregations, and windowing functions directly in their streaming queries. Now you can calculate metrics over time (for example, a 30-minute average) to power your downstream applications and AI agents with much richer, real-time signals.

    Try out our featurehere and share your feedback with bq-continuous-queries-feedback@google.com!

  • Synthetic data generator tool is available for Managed Service for Kafka

    You’ve launched your first Kafka cluster. Now what? The next thing to do is to produce some data to the cluster, but that involves modifying a client application somewhere or spinning up a virtual machine. The synthetic data generator tool, now generally available, can start sending mock data to your cluster in 3 clicks, and will get data streaming into your cluster in less than two minutes. The perfect utility for those moments you just want to test your cluster and new features. Try our quickstart today!

  • Dataflow pipeline updates are faster & more flexible

    Dataflow pipeline updates can now stop-and-replace pipelines, a major addition to the existing in-place-update feature. The new parallel pipeline option accelerates the migration between the old & new pipeline, resulting in reduced disruption to your business. You can also set a timeout on drains that prevents runaway costs for your pipeliness in the event of stuck processing. This feature is generally available. Try it here!

July 6 - July 10

  • New Lakehouse managed tables now in preview

    Lakehouse tables for Apache Iceberg are now in preview and available in the console. By using Google-managed Apache Iceberg tables in Lakehouse, you can eliminate the overhead of maintaining duplicate data pipelines and complex synchronization logic between BigQuery and open-source engines. This unified table format delivers native, multi-engine read and write interoperability, allowing you to run concurrent DML/DDL operations across diverse analytics tools on a single, shared storage layer.  Built-in automated table management handles painful background optimization tasks like compaction and partition tuning, freeing up your team to focus on building rather than managing storage maintenance.

June 1 - June 5

  • Beyond the Query: Powering AI Agents with Bigtable, Firestore & Memorystore

    Discover the latest advancements in Google Cloud's NoSQL Database portfolio, including Bigtable, Firestore, and Memorystore. This series is designed for a broad audience: whether you are exploring these databases for the first time or are an existing user looking to leverage the new capabilities announced at Next '26.

    Register here to secure your spot!

  • Cloud Engineer's AI Toolkit Workshops: Solve data-driven challenges with BigQuery, AlloyDB, Gemini and more. Hosted by Google Cloud Labs, this highly technical event is built specifically for Platform Engineers, SREs, and cloud infrastructure teams ready to bridge the gap between AI prototypes and production-grade deployments. Look out for more locations coming soon

    Toronto - June 25 (Data Cloud) | RSVP Here

    Chicago - June 30 (Data Cloud) | RSVP Here

  • Start a 10-day Bigtable free trial with a 1 node SSD cluster and up to 500GB of storage capacity. With no credit card required to start, you can easily ingest workloads and manage workloads that require low-latency, high-throughput, and predictable access. Plus, new Google Cloud customers get $300 in free credits on signup.

May 11 - May 15

  • Managed Service for Apache Airflow has launched a wave of new features, including the general availability of Airflow 3.1, AI-powered agentic troubleshooting, a new managed Airflow MCP Server for custom agent integration, and declarative YAML-based orchestration pipelines—discover all the details in the full blog post.

April 20 - April 24

  • Google-built ODBC Driver for BigQuery is now available in Preview

    We are excited to announce the launch of the new, Google-built ODBC driver for BigQuery. This new open-source driver provides a direct, high-performance connection for applications to BigQuery and is developed entirely in-house by Google.Download a new driver and connect your application to BigQuery.

April 13 - April 17

  • We announced we are reintroducing Data Studio to play a significant role in the AI era, expanding from data visualizations and reports to host BigQuery conversational agents and data apps built in Colab notebooks.
  • We announced BigQuery Graph is now available in preview, offering an easy-to-use, highly scalable graph analytics solution, empowering data professionals to model, analyze and visualize massive-scale relationships in an entirely new way.

April 6 - April 10

  • We introduced Conversational Analytics for Looker Embedded environments, enabling users to add natural language experiences to their own custom data-driven applications, powered by Gemini. 
  • We expanded Looker’s capabilities for faster ad-hoc analysis, with the introduction of self-service Explores, enabling you to bring your own data to Looker’s semantic layer and gain instant access to insights in a governed data environment.

March 23 - March 27

  • We showed you how you can scale your reads with Cloud SQL autoscaling read pools. This feature allows you to provision multiple read replicas that are accessible via a single read endpoint and to dynamically adjust your read capability based on real-time application needs. 
  • Our customers are leveraging the full power of Conversational Analytics and Looker to drive major business and technical breakthroughs in the AI era. Companies like Telenor, Pet Circle, Fluent Commerce, Lighthouse Intelligence, Wego, and ROLLER are turning data into insights and actions, grounded by Looker’s semantic layer.

March 16 - March 20

  • We introduced an enhanced Gemini assistant in BigQuery Studio, transforming the agent from a code assistant into a fully context-aware analytics partner.

February 23 - February 27

  • We introduced managed and remote MCP support for Google Cloud databases, including AlloyDB, Spanner, Cloud SQL, Bigtable and Firestore, to power the next generation of agents. This announcement extends the ability for AI models to plan, build, and solve complex problems, connecting to the database tools our customers leverage daily as the backbone of their work environment.

  • We outlined how you can build a conversational agent in BigQuery using the Conversational Analytics API to help you build context-aware agents that can understand natural language, query your BigQuery data, and deliver answers in text, tables, and visual charts.

February 16 - February 20

  • Our customers are leveraging the full power of Looker to drive major business and technical breakthroughs. Companies like Arrive, Audika, Carousell, Framebridge, GumGum, Intel, Overdose Digital, Ocean Network Express, Subskribe and Promevo are leveraging Looker’s newest AI-driven capabilities, including Conversational Analytics, to transform data to insights and actions, and empower their entire organization with a single source of truth, powered by Looker’s semantic layer.

February 2 - February 6

  • Join us on March 4 for our webinar, Win Your AI Strategy with Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus, to learn how to power your generative AI workloads with 3x higher performance and 99.99% availability. Register today to discover how to build a scalable, enterprise-grade foundation for your most demanding AI applications.

January 26 - January 30

  • We introduced Conversational Analytics in BigQuery, which allows users to analyze data using natural language. Conversational Analytics in BigQuery is an intelligent agent that generates, executes and visualizes answers grounded in your business context directly in BigQuery Studio, making data insights for data professionals more conversational.
  • We outlined how data products have become the foundation for AI agents, providing the context needed to make autonomous agents reliable and trusted for real business use, backed by organized business logic and semantic understanding.
  • We highlighted how you can supercharge data analytics workflows, and outlined Google Cloud’s AI agent offerings for data engineering, data science, and development tools, so you can integrate agentic workflows in your applications, empower your teams and speed discovery.

January 19 - January 23

  • We have fundamentally reimagined Firestore with pipeline operations for Enterprise edition. Experience a powerful new engine featuring over a hundred new query features, index-less queries, new index types, and observability tooling to improve query performance. Seamlessly migrate using built-in tools and leverage Firestore’s existing differentiated serverless foundation, virtually unlimited scale, and industry-leading SLA. Join a community of 600K developers to craft expressive applications that maximize the benefits of rich queryability, real-time listen queries, robust offline caching, and cutting-edge AI-assistive coding integrations.

  • Introducing Google Cloud SQL on MSSQLTips: We are highlighting a new technical guide published on MSSQLTips titled "Introducing Google Cloud SQL." This article serves as an essential resource for SQL Server administrators and developers exploring Google Cloud's fully managed database service. It provides a detailed overview of Cloud SQL capabilities, including high availability, security integration, and the seamless transition of on-premises SQL Server workloads to the cloud, making it an ideal resource for those planning their migration strategy.

  • We are excited to announce the Public Preview of Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) integration with Cloud SQL for SQL Server. Designed to tackle the challenge of identity sprawl in multi-cloud environments, this integration allows organizations to govern database access using their existing Microsoft identity infrastructure. Key benefits include centralized identity management, enhanced security features like Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), and simplified user administration through direct group mapping. This feature is available for SQL Server 2022 and supports both public and private IP configurations.

January 12 - January 16

  • Google-built JDBC Driver for BigQuery is now available in Preview

    We are excited to announce the launch of the new, Google-built JDBC driver for BigQuery. This new open-source driver provides a direct, high-performance connection for Java applications to BigQuery and is developed entirely in-house by Google.Download a new driver and connect your Java application to BigQuery.
  • Troubleshoot Airflow tasks instantly with Gemini Cloud Assist investigations: Cloud Composer just got smarter. We are excited to announce that Gemini Cloud Assist investigations are now available directly within Cloud Composer 3. Instead of manually sifting through raw logs, you can now simply click "Investigate" on a failed Airflow task. Gemini analyzes logs and task metadata to identify failure patterns—such as resource exhaustion or timeouts—and provides actionable recommendations driven by Gemini Cloud Assist to resolve the issue. This integration shifts the debugging experience from manual toil to automated root cause analysis, significantly reducing the time required to restore your pipelines. Learn more about AI-assisted troubleshooting.
